name: useEffect()
desc: Runs the callback after React commits the render. Use it for work outside React: network, timers, listeners, the document. Return a cleanup function for anything the callback started.

name: dependency array
desc: Lists the values the callback reads. Empty array means once, a filled array means after the first render and whenever one value changes, no array means every render.

name: cleanup function
desc: The returned function runs before the next run of the same effect and once on unmount. Use it to stop whatever the effect started.

name: StrictMode double run
desc: In development StrictMode mounts, runs effects, runs cleanups, then runs effects again. Production runs them once. A corrected effect must survive both runs.
body:
Two log lines in the console during development are not a bug in your component. They are the point of StrictMode: it exposes effects that are unsafe to run twice.

Symptoms that show up under StrictMode and nowhere else:

- The list is fetched twice and the server logs two GET requests, because nothing aborts the first one.
- The counter jumps by two after one click, because the effect registered two listeners or two intervals.
- A POST creates the booking twice, because there is no idempotency key and no cleanup that cancels it.

Do not delete StrictMode from `main.jsx`. Fix the effect: abort the request, remove the listener, or guard the write with a flag that the cleanup flips. A component that survives the double run also survives fast refresh and a real remount in production.

name: fetch with AbortController
syntax: const controller = new AbortController(); fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal })
desc: Aborts the request when the effect is cleaned up. Stops the response from setting state after unmount and stops a slow response from overwriting a newer one.
body:
`abort()` makes the pending `fetch` reject with a `DOMException` whose `name` is `AbortError`. That rejection is expected and must not be shown to the user, which is why the catch checks the name before setting an error message.

One controller per effect run. A controller created outside the effect is shared by every run and aborts requests it does not own.

Aborting does not remove the need for the `response.ok` check. A 404 resolves normally, with `ok` set to false, and calling `response.json()` on it usually gives an error object that your list rendering will choke on.

name: race condition guard
syntax: let ignore = false; ... if (ignore) return; return () => { ignore = true; };
desc: Keeps an older response from overwriting a newer one when the user changes the input faster than the network answers.

name: async work inside an effect
desc: The effect callback must not be async. An async function returns a Promise, and React expects nothing or a cleanup function.
body:
The inner function also gives you a natural place for `try` and `catch`. An unhandled rejection in the effect body becomes a console error and a spinner that never stops.

If the effect needs to wait for its own cleanup, that is a sign the state should live in a parent or in a store. The effect model expects fire and forget plus a cleanup.

Do not `await` the inner call either. Awaiting would make the callback async again and delay the cleanup until the request finished, which may be after unmount.

name: interval in an effect
syntax: useEffect(() => { const id = setInterval(fn, ms); return () => clearInterval(id); }, [])
desc: Starts a repeating timer after mount and clears it on unmount. Use the functional state update inside the tick to avoid a stale value.
body:
`setSeconds(seconds + 1)` inside the interval reads `seconds` from the render that created the timer, which is `0`. The display counts 0, 1, 1, 1 and looks frozen. The functional form receives the current value and has no stale read.

The conditional `return` before the setup is legal: the hook is called on every render, only the body changes. What must never be conditional is the `useEffect` call itself.

With `[running]` in the array, starting and stopping creates and clears exactly one interval. With `[]`, pressing Start twice leaves two intervals running and the counter speeds up.

name: subscribe and unsubscribe
syntax: useEffect(() => { target.addEventListener(type, handler); return () => target.removeEventListener(type, handler); }, [deps])
desc: Adds a listener or store subscription after mount and removes it on unmount and before every re-run. The handler must be the same reference in both calls.

name: WebSocket in an effect
syntax: const socket = new WebSocket(url); return () => socket.close();
desc: Opens the socket after mount, closes it in the cleanup, and depends on the room or url so a change reconnects to the right place.

name: derived value, no effect
desc: A value computed from props or state is calculated during render. Copying it into state with an effect costs a render and lags one step behind.
body:
The first version renders once with the old total, then again with the new one. On a slow machine that flicker is visible. It also creates a second source of truth, and the exam question about "why does the total not update" is usually this pattern.

The same rule covers filtering, sorting, counting, formatting a date, and building a query string.

One case that does need state: a value the user can edit which starts from a prop. Keep the prop as the source and store only the edit:

```jsx
const [draft, setDraft] = useState(null);
const value = draft ?? customer.first_name;
```

`useMemo` is for an expensive calculation, not for correctness. A cheap `reduce` over fifty rows does not need it.

name: manual reload of an effect
desc: An effect runs when a dependency changes. To run it on demand, add a counter state and bump it from a Retry handler.
body:
Calling the loader directly from the click handler is also valid and often simpler, because a retry is a user action, not a state change. Use the counter when the loader needs the same setup, cleanup and guards as the automatic run, and duplicating it in the handler would mean two copies of the abort logic.

The functional increment `setReload((n) => n + 1)` is required. `setReload(reload + 1)` works only while the value is fresh, which it usually is, but the functional form has no such condition.

Do not reach for this pattern when the effect only exists because a flag changed. A handler that posts a booking is a handler, not an effect with a `submitted` dependency.

name: check response.ok
desc: fetch resolves on 404 and 500, so a missing ok check turns a server error into an empty list.

name: effect on a route parameter
desc: The route parameter is the dependency. Without it, navigating between two ids keeps the data of the first one, because the component does not remount.
body:
A route like `/hotels/:id/bookings` keeps the same component mounted when the id changes, so `useState` keeps the old array. Only the effect can notice the new parameter.

A common wrong fix is a `key` prop on the route element, which forces a remount and drops all state. It works, but it is a blunt tool: every navigation loses scroll position and form input. The dependency array is the precise one.

`useParams` returns strings. Convert to a number when the API expects one, or the request goes out as `/api/hotels/7/bookings` in one place and `/api/hotels/"7"/bookings` in another.
